vignette:
He is seventy-two now, a tall African man with a careful way of sitting, as if part of him is always braced for impact. He has been married for more than forty years, and when he talks about his life he often measures time by postings, storms, and patrols. For most of his adulthood he serves in the Coast Guard. He likes the order of the work, the routines of maintenance and inspection, the confidence that comes from knowing what to do in dangerous conditions. Before the exposure, he thinks of himself as steady, the one younger men look to when machinery fails or the weather turns.

The event happens late in his career during what is supposed to be a controlled response near a commercial vessel. There has been a leak from industrial containers in rough water, and his unit is sent to secure the area and help with evacuation. At first he remembers the scene in sharp operational details: the slap of waves against metal, shouted instructions disappearing in the wind, the sour, unnatural smell that cuts through salt air. He is wearing protective gear, but there is confusion about what exactly has spilled and whether the masks they have are enough. Someone says it is contained. Someone else says to pull back. In that moment he keeps moving because that is what he has always done.

Then the fumes hit him. He remembers his throat seizing first, then his eyes burning so hard that tears flood inside the mask. He cannot get a full breath. He hears coughing all around him and the clatter of boots on the deck. One of the younger men stumbles. He goes toward him automatically, but his own chest feels locked, as if the air has turned thick and hostile. He remembers thinking, with a clarity that still frightens him, that he may die there standing up, unable to draw in one clean breath. Later there are medics, decontamination, oxygen, bright lights in a treatment bay. What stays with him most is not only the physical terror but the betrayal of the air itself. Since then, he says, nowhere feels entirely safe.

In the months afterward, people around him focus on whether his lungs will recover, whether he can return to duty, whether the reports have been filed correctly. He tries to focus on those things too. He tells himself he has survived worse. But his body begins reacting before his mind can make sense of it. Diesel fumes at the harbor make his heart hammer. Cleaning products in a supermarket force him to abandon his cart and hurry outside. If his wife uses bleach in the bathroom, he stands in the yard breathing hard, angry with himself and unable to explain why he feels as if he is back on that deck.

Sleep becomes thin and unreliable. Some nights he startles awake coughing, certain for a few disoriented seconds that his mask has failed and no oxygen is coming. Other nights he dreams of the younger crewman reaching for him through a cloud he cannot see through. His wife tells him he fights in his sleep, flinging an arm, kicking at the sheets. He is embarrassed by her worry and says little. During the day he becomes watchful in a way that exhausts him. He scans rooms for windows, vents, exits. He notices every smell immediately and mistrusts it. At church, if incense is used, he sits near the door. At family gatherings, if someone lights charcoal or uses insect spray, he leaves early and waits in the car.

Before, he is a talkative man at work, proud of sea stories and old lessons. Afterward, he grows quiet. He avoids former colleagues because he does not want to answer questions about retirement, about the incident, about whether he froze or failed someone. He knows no one has accused him of that, yet he carries a private guilt about the younger men who were exposed with him. He replays small decisions endlessly: whether he should have ordered retreat sooner, whether he should have recognized the risk faster, whether experience should have protected them better. Sometimes he watches the news for reports about spills or industrial accidents and feels his stomach drop, as though the event is happening again in real time.

His wife notices that the sea, once his place of calm, has changed for him. He still walks near the shore, but he no longer lingers by working docks. The smell of fuel mixed with salt makes his shoulders tighten. When grandchildren ask about his Coast Guard years, he tells them older stories, safer ones, stories of rescues and navigation and discipline. He leaves out the day the air turned poisonous. Even now, speaking of it in the room, he pauses often, pressing thumb to forefinger as if grounding himself. He says he used to trust his training, his body, his instincts. Since the exposure, he feels on guard against things other people do not even notice. He misses the man who could step toward danger and think clearly. What troubles him most is that the emergency never seems fully over; part of him remains on that deck, waiting for the next breath to fail.
